modules.title: The five views of a loan
modules.subtitle: Understand the contract before the calculator
lesson: A loan joins a borrower promise to a lender asset. Amount, rate, tenor and repayment frequency describe the starting contract; fees, tranches, moratoriums and later amendments make its servicing behavior specific. A sanctioned amount is an approved limit. A confirmed disbursement creates funded exposure. They can differ.

Inspect every event through five views: business instruction, bank cash, contractual schedule, accounting movement, and control evidence. An on-time EMI is simple only when all five agree. A bank credit can be real while its borrower is unknown; a schedule can show a due amount while no cash has arrived.

Principal is unpaid funded exposure. Interest compensates time and risk; it is a separate component. A reducing-balance loan earns interest on the agreed outstanding basis. A flat-rate quotation uses original principal and does not describe the same yield as a reducing rate.

An overdraft needs utilization and limits; an EMI term loan needs dated installments. A tranche loan needs interest on confirmed drawdowns. Product choice therefore changes the model, rather than merely changing the screen label.

Worked example: ₹3,00,000 sanctioned, ₹1,20,000 disbursed, ₹20,000 principal repaid. Funded principal outstanding is ₹1,00,000, with ₹1,80,000 undisbursed sanction. Future interest is not part of principal. These quantities answer different questions.

modules.title: LOS, LMS, payments and GL
modules.subtitle: Know who owns each state transition
lesson: LOS usually manages application, underwriting, sanction and accepted terms. LMS usually manages the booked contract after disbursement: schedules, bills, receipts, allocations and servicing. CBS and specialist systems may divide these duties differently; document an explicit owner for each fact.

A controlled handoff validates final accepted terms, borrower identity references, product version, fees, rate, tenor, mandates and partner terms. Store the accepted version rather than silently applying the newest product defaults to an older offer.

Payment instructions and bank confirmations answer whether money was requested or moved. Allocation answers which loan components were cleared. Accounting records debit and credit movements; GL aggregates those movements into control accounts. One webhook should not invent all of these facts.

The monetary transaction boundary should keep allocation, loan balances and accounting event creation consistent. Downstream notifications and reporting can use a durable outbox and retry. Eventual consistency still needs completion evidence and exception ownership.

Worked trace: bank credit → reconciled receipt → borrower identification → versioned allocation → balanced sub-ledger journal → GL export acknowledgment. A failed GL export should be retried using the existing batch identity, rather than collecting the customer payment again.

modules.title: Loan math and cashflow yield
modules.subtitle: PV, EMI, IRR, APR and EIR without conflation
lesson: For monthly reducing installments, r is the monthly rate, n the payment count and P the opening principal. EMI = P × r / (1 − (1+r)^−n), with P/n when r=0. Nominal annual rate divided by twelve is a convention for this model, rather than an assertion about every product.

Each scheduled row has interest = opening principal × r, principal = EMI − interest, closing = opening − principal. This model assumes installments are paid as scheduled. If they bounce, contractual scheduled closing and actual unpaid funded exposure can diverge.

Present value discounts future cashflows. IRR is a rate that makes net present value zero; the periodic IRR depends on cashflow spacing. Annual effective yield from monthly IRR m is (1+m)^12 − 1. Simply multiplying by twelve produces a nominal annualization.

APR is a borrower cost disclosure under the applicable method and cost inclusion rules. EIR is a financial accounting yield using relevant expected contractual flows and qualifying fees or transaction costs. A generic IRR is a mathematical tool used in such calculations, not a complete regulatory APR implementation.

Worked example: lend ₹1,00,000 now and receive ₹1,10,000 in exactly one year, with no other flows: IRR is 10%. If a ₹2,000 fee is withheld so the borrower receives ₹98,000, the same repayment implies 12.2449% one-year borrower cashflow yield. This illustrative yield is not automatically the required APR for every product.

modules.title: Schedules, tranches and actual exposure
modules.subtitle: Separate expected, billed, accrued and paid
lesson: An expected schedule describes contracted future installments. Billing records what became due. Accrual records interest earned under the stated basis. Actual movements record collections and principal repayment. A shadow schedule supports simulations without changing the active contract.

Broken-period interest covers an irregular interval, such as disbursement before the first regular billing cycle. State the interest-bearing principal, rate, start/end convention and day count. Actual/365 and Actual/360 can produce different charges for identical dates.

Tranche products compute interest on confirmed funded amounts. Floating resets, principal prepayments and approved restructuring create versioned prospective schedules. Preserve the old version and the triggering event to explain historical bills.

A moratorium changes timing; it does not by itself waive interest. Accrual, separate recovery or permitted capitalization depends on explicit terms and applicable rules. A holiday shift also needs a due-date and interest convention.

Worked example: ₹1,00,000 × 12% × 10/365 = ₹328.77, rounded to paise after the calculation. At Actual/360 the same assumed ten days gives ₹333.33. If a scheduled ₹6,000 principal installment bounces, actual POS does not fall merely because the table says it should.

modules.title: Component balances and double entry
modules.subtitle: Explain every rupee without counting it twice
lesson: This module uses a simplified performing-loan lender ledger: POS includes all unpaid principal, including principal already billed. Interest and charges use separate receivables; unapplied customer cash is a liability. Institution-specific standards, EIR and impairment treatment require separate policy.

Assets increase by debit and decrease by credit. Liabilities and income increase by credit. A disbursement debits loan principal and credits bank. Earned performing-loan interest in this assumed accrual model debits interest receivable and credits interest income. Collecting already accrued interest clears the receivable; it does not recognize that income again.

Billing may reclassify principal from not-yet-due to due without changing total principal. Never add overdue principal to a POS that already includes it. Build totals from disjoint components; define gross principal, due principal, accrued/billed interest, charges, tax and unapplied credits explicitly.

Receipt in two stages: first debit bank and credit payment clearing. Then debit clearing and credit principal, interest receivable or advance liability as allocated. The second stage has no new bank debit. Direct collection templates and suspense templates are alternatives, not two cash receipts.

Worked example: POS ₹1,00,000 includes ₹10,000 overdue principal. Interest ₹2,000, charge ₹500 and assumed tax ₹90 are disjoint; customer advance is ₹1,000. Illustrative closure amount = 1,00,000 + 2,000 + 500 + 90 − 1,000 = ₹1,01,590. Adding ₹10,000 overdue principal again would overstate it.

modules.title: Receipts, suspense and advances
modules.subtitle: Cash received is only the beginning
lesson: A real bank receipt can be unidentified, identified but unallocated, allocated, or held as a borrower advance. Use distinct typed states and liabilities rather than one ambiguous suspense bucket. Receipts need source IDs, bank references, amount, value date and state history.

Under the examples here, advance EMI parks early money for future obligations. It does not immediately reduce POS or earn future interest. A valid principal prepayment is a different instruction: it reduces principal when applied and triggers the specified prospective schedule change.

Applying an advance later debits advance liability and credits the due components. Bank moved when the advance arrived, not when it is consumed. Excess after dues clear follows the stated instruction or approved default policy; never silently invent a principal prepayment.

Two independent bank receipts are two real cash events even if they relate to one EMI. A repeated notification for the same bank transaction is one receipt. This distinction is essential when NACH and UPI both succeed.

Worked example: due interest ₹2,000 and principal ₹8,000; two distinct ₹10,000 receipts arrive. Total cash is ₹20,000. After one ₹10,000 due allocation, ₹10,000 remains unapplied or refundable under policy. Interest income is not doubled simply because two payments were made.

modules.title: Waterfalls and allocation reasoning
modules.subtitle: Compare bucket-first and component-first results
lesson: A waterfall orders application of a finite payment. Specify due buckets, component priority, permitted amount, event type, asset state and effective version. No sequence is a universal RBI allocation rule; these examples are deliberately stated product policies.

Vertical allocation here means choose the oldest installment and clear its tax, charge, interest and principal before moving to the next. Horizontal allocation here means clear a component across all overdue buckets before proceeding to the next component.

The same payment can leave different oldest unpaid amounts under different policies. DPD follows the remaining relevant due amount under the defined delinquency rule; it does not automatically become zero after any cash receipt.

Allocation must conserve money: payment = applied + unapplied. Each line must be nonnegative and no greater than its component due. Reversal restores the original lines, not a newly chosen waterfall based on the current product version.

Worked example: bucket A = ₹100 charge + ₹900 interest + ₹3,000 principal; bucket B = ₹100 + ₹800 + ₹3,000. A ₹4,000 vertical payment closes A. Horizontal charge → interest → principal clears ₹200 charges and ₹1,700 interest, then ₹2,100 A principal; A still has ₹900 principal. Total dues are ₹7,900 and remaining dues ₹3,900 either way.

modules.title: Prepayment, foreclosure and settlement
modules.subtitle: Build quotes from disjoint components
lesson: A principal prepayment reduces part of funded exposure while the loan remains active. Foreclosure settles the full contractual closure amount as of a specified date. Negotiated settlement accepts less than contractual rights with an approved concession; it needs a distinct loss/waiver and reporting analysis.

Use disjoint quote components. In this module POS includes due and not-yet-due principal; add separate earned interest and charges/tax only once, subtract eligible credits once. An overdue EMI total cannot simply be added to inclusive POS because its principal overlaps.

Residual interest depends on the stated interest basis, effective rate, dates and prior billed/accrued amounts. A quote has version and validity. It is usually a simulation unless the process separately bills earned amounts. Issuing a quote is not receiving money.

Current fee eligibility requires lender category, borrower/purpose, sanction or renewal date, rate type at prepayment and relevant amount thresholds from the applicable current source. This app does not grade unverified current prepayment/KFS/penal-charge thresholds. A dated guide alone is insufficient.

Worked example: inclusive POS ₹50,000; distinct interest ₹600; assumed permitted charge ₹200 and illustrative tax ₹36; eligible advance ₹1,000. Quote ₹49,836. A ₹49,000 receipt leaves ₹836 unpaid under an exact-payment policy. Financial closure remains pending; approved tolerances must be explicit rather than invented.

modules.title: Delinquency, reversal and recovery
modules.subtitle: Track arrears separately from losses
lesson: DPD measures age of the oldest relevant unpaid obligation using the institution/product rule and local date cutoff. The exercises here define DPD as date difference from oldest unpaid principal or interest due; charges alone are excluded unless explicitly stated. This is an illustrative calculation, not a universal asset-classification rule.

A failed collection does not repay principal. A chargeback reverses a prior actual receipt/allocation through controlled events and can restore dues. DPD should then be recomputed from the restored due dates, rather than simply set to the transaction date.

Regulatory NPA, contractual delinquency and financial accounting impairment are related but distinct. Applicable entity, product and accounting standards determine recognition and provisioning. Do not convert an illustrative more-than-90-day scenario into every product's current statutory rule.

Under a stated allowance/write-off policy, provision expense increases an allowance; an approved write-off removes the specified asset against allowance or expense. An accounting write-off does not itself prove legal release of the borrower. Recovery needs a surviving rights trail and the applicable accounting policy.

Worked example: principal due ₹5,000 and interest due ₹1,000 on 1 June. On 11 June, both remain unpaid: defined DPD is ten days. If ₹1,000 clears only interest, principal remains aged from 1 June. If all relevant dues clear, defined DPD becomes zero. A later reversal restores the original due state for recalculation.

modules.title: Co-lending shares and escrow
modules.subtitle: Principal ratio is not interest entitlement
lesson: Co-lending adds lender-share and settlement views to the borrower contract. For an illustrative two-lender loan, preserve borrower obligations, lender A principal/interest, lender B principal/interest, and escrow cash/settlement liabilities. Do not treat a partner report as a substitute for a share ledger.

In the assumed commercial example, A funds 80% at 10.5% and B funds 20% at 18%. Borrower blended rate is 12%. A month of interest on ₹1,00,000 is ₹1,000: A earns ₹700 and B ₹300. Principal repayment follows 80:20, but interest follows the share balance times each share rate.

If the receipt has ₹4,000 principal plus ₹1,000 interest, A entitlement is ₹3,200 + ₹700 = ₹3,900; B is ₹800 + ₹300 = ₹1,100. Splitting total cash 80:20 would produce ₹4,000 and ₹1,000 and misallocate interest under these assumptions.

Escrow receipt, allocation and payout are distinct. A settled borrower receipt can clear dues while a partner payout remains pending. Failed internal payout leaves a partner liability and exception; it must not automatically make the borrower pay twice.

Current CLA rules are entity-scoped. New in-scope arrangements governed by current Part B have verified retention, booking, escrow, share-account and classification controls. Legacy arrangements need transition analysis. The Sources screen records the current successors and held topics; the controls module tests only approved scoped claims.

modules.title: Reconciliation and reliable event processing
modules.subtitle: Retry and reverse without inventing cash
lesson: Reconcile each layer with aligned scope and dates: bank cash to receipts; receipt to allocation plus residual; allocations to component movements and accounting; sub-ledger to GL; lender entitlements to settled payouts plus outstanding payables. Totals alone can hide cross-loan errors.

An idempotency key identifies one economic event across delivery retries. Enforce uniqueness durably. Reusing the same key with a different amount or loan is a conflict requiring investigation, not permission to overwrite the original.

Use transactional outbox to persist downstream work alongside the authoritative transaction. Consumers need deduplication too: at-least-once delivery can repeat. Kafka or a queue is not by itself proof of ledger completeness.

A saga coordinates multi-step operations with durable states. Payout instruction, bank debit and confirmation need separate identities. Reversal adds linked compensating events. Allocation-only correction can leave cash untouched; chargeback or refund actually changes cash.

Worked example: customer paid gross ₹10,000, gateway settles ₹9,850 after ₹150 contractual merchant fee. If the borrower is entitled to gross credit under the stated policy, record bank ₹9,850 plus fee expense ₹150 against clearing ₹10,000. Giving only ₹9,850 borrower credit confuses merchant cost with borrower obligation.

modules.title: Current Indian controls and source judgment
modules.subtitle: Scoped rules, evidence and effective dates
lesson: Rule checked: 4 October 2026. The 28 November 2025 RBI consolidation withdrew listed earlier instruments while preserving prior actions and consolidating obligations. Current study therefore uses entity-specific successor directions. The supplied June 2026 handbook remains an educational source, with dated citations and corrected examples.

For an in-scope CLA governed by current commercial-bank Part B, each participating commercial bank retains at least 10% of an individual loan; shares are booked without avoidable delay and no later than fifteen calendar days after disbursement. If the originating bank cannot transfer the partner exposure share within the deadline, the loan stays with the originating bank and a later transfer follows Part A. Scope and transition rules must be checked before applying these lessons to an actual entity.

Current bank CLA rules require bank-held escrow, share reporting to CIC, and coordinated SMA/NPA classification for default in the CLA exposure. Classification information is exchanged near-real-time, no later than end of next working day. NBFC CLA successors also require separate borrower share accounts and a funding-share-weighted borrower rate.

For an in-scope NBFC digital loan under current Credit Facilities Directions, outsourcing leaves regulatory responsibility with the NBFC. LSP control over loan fund flows, directly or indirectly, is prohibited. Routing exceptions do not permit LSP control. Routing has specified exceptions, including inter-lender co-lending and other enumerated cases; avoid absolute no-exception slogans.

Current prepayment, KFS and penal-charge successor details are held out of current-law scoring because their full texts were not accessible to the independent reviewer. General fee eligibility, disclosure versioning and no-double-counting lessons here are design principles, not certification of a live legal matrix. Sources lists the held texts and historical lineage.

cards.front: What are the five views of a loan event?
cards.back: Business, cash, schedule, accounting and control evidence must explain the same event.

cards.front: Sanction versus disbursement: what creates funded exposure?
cards.back: Confirmed disbursement creates funded principal; sanction records approved lending capacity.

cards.front: How do principal and interest differ?
cards.back: Principal tracks the unpaid amount funded. Interest is separately earned under time and rate conventions.

cards.front: Why can two 12% rate quotes have different costs?
cards.back: Flat and reducing conventions use different interest bases, and fees and timing affect cashflow yield.

cards.front: What determines whether early cash is a prepayment?
cards.back: Borrower instruction, contract and applicable policy determine advance versus principal treatment.

cards.front: How does an overdraft differ from an EMI term loan?
cards.back: An overdraft tracks utilization, drawing limits and daily interest rather than a fixed amortization table alone.

cards.front: What does a principal-only moratorium defer?
cards.back: It defers principal obligations; interest treatment must be read separately.

cards.front: Why is closure a workflow?
cards.back: Financial balances, cash, customer documents and operational obligations need separate controlled completion.

cards.front: Why are funded exposure and book carrying amount different?
cards.back: Carrying amount can reflect fee amortization and impairment; funded exposure measures principal rights.

cards.front: What evidence makes a balance explainable?
cards.back: Trace source events, component movements, rule versions and effective dates to the displayed balance.

cards.front: What does LOS normally own?
cards.back: Application, underwriting, sanction and final offer acceptance before controlled booking.

cards.front: What does LMS normally own?
cards.back: Booked loan servicing: schedules, dues, allocations, balances and servicing mutations.

cards.front: What makes booking handoff controlled?
cards.back: Validate and preserve the final accepted terms, identities, product and disclosure versions.

cards.front: What is a system of record?
cards.back: The defined authoritative owner of a fact, with controlled changes and reconciliation to other views.

cards.front: Where should monetary consistency be strongest?
cards.back: Allocation, component balances and accounting event generation should share a controlled transaction boundary.

cards.front: What is safe to publish through an outbox?
cards.back: Persist downstream work with the monetary transaction, then deliver and retry it separately.

cards.front: Why is rail success not always final cash proof?
cards.back: Rail response, settlement, bank statement and reconciliation can describe distinct stages.

cards.front: What should a GL control account reconcile to?
cards.back: The matching aggregate of account-level sub-ledger movements or balances, using aligned dimensions and cutoff.

cards.front: Why separate loan state from workflow state?
cards.back: A pending partner payout or document task is not the same fact as a borrower debt balance.

cards.front: How should a boundary integration be evaluated?
cards.back: Prove ownership, IDs, duplicate handling, error recovery, cutoff and reconciliation with actual scenarios.

cards.front: What is present value?
cards.back: Future cash discounted to the valuation date using a stated periodic rate and timing.

cards.front: What is the monthly rate in this nominal model?
cards.back: The stated nominal annual rate divided by twelve for monthly reducing calculations.

cards.front: How is the first EMI interest component calculated?
cards.back: Opening funded principal multiplied by the specified periodic rate.

cards.front: What does zero-rate EMI become?
cards.back: With no fees or interest and equal installments, payment is principal divided by count.

cards.front: What does IRR solve?
cards.back: The discount rate at which the signed dated cashflows have zero NPV.

cards.front: Why do withheld fees change borrower cashflow yield?
cards.back: The borrower receives less net cash but may owe the same future payments.

cards.front: How do nominal and effective annual rates differ?
cards.back: Monthly compounding gives effective annual growth of (1+m)^12 − 1.

cards.front: Why are APR and EIR separate measures?
cards.back: Borrower disclosure cost and lender accounting yield can use different inclusion rules and purposes.

cards.front: What is a limitation of an IRR solver?
cards.back: Non-conventional cashflows can have multiple roots or no suitable unique IRR.

cards.front: Why must rounding be specified?
cards.back: Billing, display and internal precision boundaries can change paise residuals.

cards.front: What is the expected schedule?
cards.back: A contractual projection of future amounts and dates under stated assumptions.

cards.front: What distinguishes billing from accrual?
cards.back: Billing creates payable dues; accrual tracks earned interest on its specified basis.

cards.front: Why use a shadow schedule?
cards.back: Simulate proposed changes without overwriting the active schedule.

cards.front: What inputs define broken-period interest?
cards.back: Funded principal, rate, interval convention and day-count basis.

cards.front: How does Actual/360 differ here?
cards.back: For the same amount, rate and actual days, denominator 360 produces more interest than 365.

cards.front: How do tranches affect interest?
cards.back: The specified interest base follows confirmed funded amounts, not the whole sanction.

cards.front: What should a rate reset preserve?
cards.back: Prior schedule versions, effective date, event, reason and approved new prospective terms.

cards.front: How do EMI and tenor reduction differ?
cards.back: At a lower POS, holding tenor lowers EMI; holding EMI generally shortens tenor under otherwise unchanged terms.

cards.front: Why test holiday shifts?
cards.back: Due-date movement and interest treatment are separate product conventions.

cards.front: What proves actual POS after a bounce?
cards.back: Confirmed funded principal minus actual principal repayments and approved principal reductions under the chosen ledger model.

cards.front: What increases a lender loan asset?
cards.back: A debit increases an asset; confirmed disbursement normally debits principal and credits bank in this simplified model.

cards.front: What does accrual do in the stated performing-loan model?
cards.back: It records earned interest receivable and income before cash collection.

cards.front: What happens when already accrued interest is collected?
cards.back: Bank increases and the existing interest receivable clears; earned income is not recognized twice.

cards.front: Can overdue principal be added to inclusive POS?
cards.back: No. If POS already includes due principal, adding it again double counts that exposure.

cards.front: Why is principal billing a reclassification in this model?
cards.back: Moving principal from not-yet-due to due changes presentation, not total funded exposure.

cards.front: What is clearing-stage allocation's cash impact?
cards.back: Bank was debited at receipt; allocation debits clearing and credits the settled components.

cards.front: Why is unapplied customer cash a liability here?
cards.back: The lender holds cash pending allocation or refund; it is not automatically earned income.

cards.front: What does an impairment allowance do?
cards.back: It reduces net carrying amount separately from gross exposure under the stated allowance model.

cards.front: Are balanced journals sufficient proof of correctness?
cards.back: Balance is necessary but wrong accounts, duplication or wrong economic events can still balance.

cards.front: How should a posted error be reversed?
cards.back: Add a controlled compensating journal linked to the original, then post any correct replacement.

cards.front: What is an unidentified receipt?
cards.back: Bank cash is confirmed but no borrower/loan attribution is established.

cards.front: What is identified but unallocated cash?
cards.back: The borrower is known but application to components is pending or blocked.

cards.front: Why is advance EMI not immediate principal repayment?
cards.back: Under advance policy, cash is held for later dues; instruction and contract determine application.

cards.front: How is advance consumption posted?
cards.back: Debit advance liability and credit due components without another bank debit.

cards.front: What does an explicit principal prepayment change?
cards.back: It reduces applied principal exposure and creates the stated revised prospective schedule.

cards.front: How should unexplained excess be handled?
cards.back: Preserve the excess in a typed unapplied/refund state pending the governing policy or instruction.

cards.front: How are duplicate webhook and duplicate payment different?
cards.back: Repeated reference for one transaction is a retry; distinct settled bank credits are separate cash events.

cards.front: What if NACH and UPI both really settle?
cards.back: Record both cash receipts; allocate according to obligations and park/refund the excess under policy.

cards.front: How is an approved excess refund recorded here?
cards.back: Debit the borrower payable or unapplied liability and credit bank; link to source receipt and approval.

cards.front: Why age suspense balances?
cards.back: Unresolved cash needs owners, reasons, aging and reconciliation; a balanced GL does not resolve attribution.

cards.front: What is vertical allocation in these lessons?
cards.back: Choose oldest installment first, then its ordered components before the next installment.

cards.front: What is horizontal allocation in these lessons?
cards.back: Clear the chosen component across buckets before the next component.

cards.front: What is the allocation conservation equation?
cards.back: Receipt equals allocated amount plus unapplied residual.

cards.front: Why can waterfalls change DPD outcomes?
cards.back: They leave different oldest unpaid due components; the specified DPD basis determines aging.

cards.front: Why store the waterfall version?
cards.back: Reproduce the actual allocation using rules effective for that event.

cards.front: How does waiver change allocation capacity?
cards.back: An approved waiver removes the corresponding due before later allocation.

cards.front: What is a hybrid waterfall?
cards.back: An explicitly defined combination of component and bucket priorities, rather than a vague label.

cards.front: What must allocation reversal restore?
cards.back: Original affected component amounts and linked accounting, with an audited reversal event.

cards.front: How should a component allocation be capped?
cards.back: Apply the smaller of cash available and eligible due, then continue or park residual.

cards.front: Why should policy examples be labeled?
cards.back: Commercial order, tax assumptions and aging rules vary; stated examples do not establish universal law.

cards.front: How is part-prepayment different from foreclosure?
cards.back: Part-prepayment reduces principal while the loan remains active; foreclosure clears the full contractual closure obligation.

cards.front: What makes a quote reproducible?
cards.back: As-of date, validity, balances, component formulas and schedule/rate/rule versions.

cards.front: Does creating a shadow quote itself move cash?
cards.back: No cash is received merely by calculating a quote.

cards.front: How do you avoid principal overlap in a closure quote?
cards.back: If POS already includes due principal, add only distinct interest, charges and eligible adjustments.

cards.front: How are eligible advances used in the example quote?
cards.back: Subtract the eligible unapplied credit once or apply it once before quoting.

cards.front: What does an expired quote require?
cards.back: Recompute or validate under a controlled process; preserve the old quote and receipt state.

cards.front: What is the result of short-paying an exact quote?
cards.back: Under the stated exact-payment policy, residual dues remain and closure is pending.

cards.front: What makes settlement distinct?
cards.back: Approved acceptance of less than contractual dues requires concession accounting and appropriate status analysis.

cards.front: How should foreclosure excess be treated?
cards.back: Clear owed amounts and record remaining real cash as borrower payable/unapplied pending refund.

cards.front: What is needed before implementing a live charge rule?
cards.back: Read the current applicable source and capture entity class, date, purpose, rate and other eligibility attributes.

cards.front: What does DPD measure in these exercises?
cards.back: Calendar-date age of the oldest unpaid principal or interest due, with stated cutoff and no charge-only aging.

cards.front: Does a failed payment reduce funded exposure?
cards.back: No principal repayment occurs merely from a failed payment attempt.

cards.front: What if only interest clears under the defined DPD rule?
cards.back: Unpaid aged principal still keeps the oldest relevant bucket open.

cards.front: Are NPA and accounting credit impairment synonyms?
cards.back: No. Test their applicable regulatory and accounting definitions separately.

cards.front: How does a chargeback affect allocation?
cards.back: Reverse the relevant cash/allocation and restore affected dues through linked compensating events.

cards.front: What is memo interest under the illustrative policy?
cards.back: Recovery tracking separate from recognized P&L income under that specified policy.

cards.front: What is an allowance in the stated model?
cards.back: A contra-asset estimate booked separately from gross principal.

cards.front: Does accounting write-off always cancel legal recovery?
cards.back: No; legal rights and borrower release need separate evidence and policy.

cards.front: How is a post-write-off recovery recognized?
cards.back: Use the applicable institution's policy; do not invent one universal recovery-income entry.

cards.front: How do delinquency and collections workflow differ?
cards.back: DPD is a calculated obligation state; contact attempts and promises are operational workflow facts.

cards.front: What four views make the example co-lending model useful?
cards.back: Borrower obligations, both lender share ledgers, and escrow/settlement cash.

cards.front: How is the assumed blended rate computed?
cards.back: Funding-share-weighted lender rates under the stated terms.

cards.front: Why is interest share different from principal share?
cards.back: Interest is share balance times lender rate; different rates change the entitlement proportions.

cards.front: How much interest belongs to B in the example?
cards.back: ₹20,000 share principal at 18% annual/12 earns ₹300 per month.

cards.front: How is principal allocated under the stated 80:20 rule?
cards.back: Split principal repayment by the agreed principal ratio and track rounding residual.

cards.front: What is combined entitlement in the example?
cards.back: Add each lender's principal share and its separately calculated interest share.

cards.front: What remains when partner payout fails?
cards.back: The borrower allocation stays supported by real receipt; partner payable remains for retry and recon.

cards.front: How should co-lending rounding conserve cash?
cards.back: Round one allocated share and give the exact paise residual to the designated other share under policy.

cards.front: How should advances be shared?
cards.back: Follow the stated agreement: hold borrower-level or share-level liabilities, with consistent future application.

cards.front: What reconciles share principal to borrower POS?
cards.back: Sum of lender principal shares must equal borrower inclusive POS under the shared model.

cards.front: What is economic idempotency?
cards.back: One monetary event is recorded once even when the same delivery is retried.

cards.front: What should happen on a conflicting duplicate key?
cards.back: Detect and hold the conflict; do not mutate the original economic event silently.

cards.front: What does a transactional outbox solve?
cards.back: It closes the gap between committed monetary state and lost downstream publication.

cards.front: Why must downstream consumers deduplicate?
cards.back: Reliable at-least-once delivery can repeat already delivered events.

cards.front: What distinguishes allocation reversal from cash reversal?
